newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore votes as PM puts prestige on line.
newsitem.headline: Singapore votes as PM puts prestige on line.

text.p: Polls opened on Thursday in Singapore's general election in which Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong has put his prestige on the line even though his party is assured of staying in power.
Goh's People's Action Party (PAP) has already been handed a victory because the opposition is contesting just 36 of parliament's 83 seats.
But Goh, who sees losing even one seat to an opposition party as a defeat, is waging an all-out effort for a PAP win in the multi-member Cheng San constituency.
Before parliament was dissolved to prepare for the elections, opposition parties held just four seats in the 81-member parliament. Redrawn constituency boundaries have added two seats.
The campaign ended with law suits flying late on Wednesday and the PAP focusing its guns on one opposition candidate in Cheng San.
Goh, who was himself returned unopposed in his own multi-member constituency on December 23, was in Cheng San to greet voters when polls opened at 8 a.m. (0000 GMT) on Thursday.

He told a campaign rally on Wednesday night he would sue Cheng San candidate Tang Liang Hong of the Workers' Party (WP), a man he accused of being a "Chinese chauvinist", endangering Singapore's multi-racial society.
WP leader Joshua Jeyaretnam said Tang would sue Goh and had already made a complaint to police alleging defamation.
"If we lose (here), the whole leadership in the government loses," senior PAP leader Lee Kuan Yew told Wednesday's rally.
Polls close at 8 p.m. (1200 GMT) and overall results were not expected until after midnight (1600 GMT). Nearly 800,000 voters were due to vote in the contested seats. Voting was compulsory.
Goh said a strong showing in the contested seats was vital for his future and for Singapore.
He has used a multi-billion dollar programme to upgrade public housing to emphasise his party's ability for economic management and to lure voters away from the opposition.
Goh has said constituencies that return opposition candidates would miss out on the programme and become slums in 20 to 30 years' time.
Setbacks would also mean other countries concluding he had been weakened and asking who would succeed him, he said.
"So they would speculate as to the stability of Singapore."
Goh made plain from the beginning of the campaign he did not wish the opposition to increase its four seats in parliament.
Cheng San has five seats at stake in a winner-take-all vote and political analysts said that was where the opposition had the best chance.
Goh, calling Tang an extremist, said his views could threaten harmony in Singapore, which is 77 percent ethnic Chinese and has significant minorities of Malays and Indians.
It is an emotive issue in a country where strong memories remain of racial riots in the 1960s.
The PAP has been in power since 1959 and has helped develop Singapore into a prosperous city where the average per capita income is higher than in Britain, the old colonial power.
The opposition, which had no representation in parliament until 1981, did not challenge in a majority of seats this time to reassure voters the PAP, and their prosperity, was not in danger.
The five opposition parties said they were fighting for an alternative voice in parliament and a check on the PAP's power.
